Pamphylia
pam-FIL-ee-uh
proper noun (a region of Asia Minor)
Greek Pamphylia, perhaps “of all tribes,” a coastal region of southern Asia Minor; the district through which Paul passed on his missionary journeys.

📖 Biblical Definition

Pamphylia was a coastal region of southern Asia Minor, lying between Lycia and Cilicia, with Perga as its chief inland city and Attalia as its port. It figures in the Acts as a district Paul traversed in his missionary labours. On the first journey, when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia, and there John Mark departed from them and returned to Jerusalem—a withdrawal that later occasioned the sharp contention between Paul and Barnabas. Returning from the highlands of Pisidia, they preached the word in Perga and went down to Attalia. Devout men from Pamphylia were among the multitude at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost who heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue. And in his last voyage Paul sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia on his way as a prisoner to Rome. The dictionary notes Pamphylia chiefly to ground the apostolic mission in real and traceable geography, and for one solemn lesson it carries: it was at Perga in Pamphylia that John Mark forsook the work, and this defection became the occasion of a painful breach between two faithful men. Yet the grace of God restored Mark, who is later commended as profitable for the ministry and became the writer of a Gospel. Pamphylia thus witnesses both to the cost of turning back from the Lord's work and to the mercy that restores the fallen servant who is recovered to usefulness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A coastal region of southern Asia Minor, with Perga its chief city, traversed by Paul on his journeys (Acts 13:13; 14:24); the place where John Mark forsook the work, occasioning a breach later healed by grace.

PAMPHYLIA, proper noun. A coastal region of southern Asia Minor between Lycia and Cilicia.

Perga was its chief inland city and Attalia its port.

Paul came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John Mark departed from the work (Acts 13:13).

Returning from Pisidia, the apostles preached in Perga (Acts 14:24-25).

Devout men of Pamphylia heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

📖 Key Scripture

Ac 13:13 — "Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem."

Ac 14:24 — "And after they had passed throughout Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia."

Ac 2:10 — "Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,"

Ac 27:5 — "And when we had sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the critical doubt cast on the historical reliability of Acts' geography and the loss of the moral lesson of Mark's defection and restoration.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the historical reliability of the book of Acts. Skeptical scholarship has often treated Luke's travel narratives as loose or legendary, but the precise and verifiable geography—Pamphylia, Perga, Attalia, the sea-lanes to Myra—has repeatedly been vindicated, and Luke stands as a careful and accurate historian. The dictionary affirms the trustworthiness of the sacred record: the apostolic mission unfolded in real places that can be traced on a map.

Pamphylia also carries a moral lesson the dictionary will not pass over. It was at Perga that John Mark forsook the work and returned to Jerusalem, a defection so serious that Paul refused to take him on the next journey, and the disagreement parted Paul and Barnabas. Yet the story does not end in failure: Mark was restored, and Paul at the last called him profitable for the ministry. The dictionary marks both edges—the real cost of turning back from the Lord's service, and the grace that recovers the fallen servant and makes him useful again. The young man who left the work in Pamphylia became, by mercy, the writer of a Gospel.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek Pamphylia, perhaps “of all tribes” (pan, all; phyle, tribe); a Roman province of mixed peoples on the southern coast of Asia Minor.

expand to see more

Pamphylia, Greek, perhaps “of all tribes,” from pan (all) and phyle (tribe).

Perga, the chief inland city, where John Mark turned back.

Attalia, the port city of the region, named for Attalus of Pergamum.

Bordered by Lycia to the west and Cilicia to the east on the southern coast.

A district of Paul's first and last journeys recorded in Acts.

Usage

"The teacher traced Paul's steps through Pamphylia to show the apostolic mission in real geography."

"He noted that Mark forsook the work at Perga in Pamphylia, yet was later restored to usefulness."

"She marked Luke's exact place-names as evidence of the historical reliability of Acts."
